title: Ravana rides out
hookLine: the king finally comes himself; the inner enemies that grow back
carry: six inner enemies, and they grow back
last: TAMAS: SEEING WHAT'S RIGHT, SLEEPING THROUGH IT.

cards: For the whole war, Ravana has sent other people. Generals. Sons.
His giant brother. One by one, they've fallen. Kumbhakarna is gone.
Now even Indrajit, his great son, the master of illusion, has been killed by Lakshmana. There's nobody left to send.
So the king of Lanka puts on his armor, climbs into his chariot, and rides out through the gates himself. Ten heads. Twenty arms.

teach.b: It's easy to make Ravana a cartoon, and the Ramayana doesn't.

In the tradition he's a great scholar, learned in the Vedas, and a fierce devotee of Shiva; a hymn to Shiva's dance, the Shiva Tandava Stotram, is traditionally said to be his. Tradition makes him a veena player too.

He's brave, and a real king to his people. And he took another man's wife by force and wouldn't give her back when everyone he trusted begged him to. That's the tragedy: all that greatness, bent around one refusal.
Even his name carries a story. In the tradition, he once tried to lift Shiva's mountain, Kailasa, and Shiva pressed it down with one toe, pinning him.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO MADE THE WORLDS CRY OUT.
teach.b: Ravana roared so loudly the worlds shook, and Shiva, in the Uttara Kanda's telling, named him Ravana: the one who made the worlds cry out. Now the fight.
Rama cuts off one of Ravana's heads with an arrow, and another grows back in its place. He cuts another. It grows back.

Hindu teaching has a name for what keeps growing back: the six inner enemies, the shadripu. Desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy. Some teachers read Ravana's ten heads as those enemies; lists differ.

Ravana had learning, devotion and courage, and it wasn't enough, because one enemy, desire, sat on the throne. That's the teaching: knowing the scriptures doesn't save you if the enemies inside are running things.
It's why, at Dussehra, when the huge ten-headed effigies burn, many families say those are what's really burning. So start small: pick one, and say its name.

how: At Dussehra, many communities in north India burn huge effigies of the ten-headed Ravana, and some teachers use the ten heads to speak about the inner faults that keep returning; the Shiva Tandava Stotram, attributed to Ravana, is chanted by devotees of Shiva.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: a hymn traditionally said to be Ravana's

s: the Ramayana shows Ravana as nothing but a monster
he's a scholar, a devotee of Shiva, a musician and a king, bent around one refusal.
Ravana's heads grow back when Rama cuts them off
over and over, which is part of why the fight is so long.
everyone lists the ten heads the same way
some teachers read them as inner faults, and the lists differ.

games.q: Ravana knew the Vedas and loved Shiva. by the teaching of the six inner enemies, why wasn't that enough?
o: desire sat on the throne, and he wouldn't give it up.
he hadn't read enough scripture yet.
his devotion to Shiva was fake all along.
games.why: learning and devotion are real gifts, but the enemies inside still have to be faced. refusing to give Sita back was desire, ruling him.

practice: Picture ten heads without fear, and give them faces you might recognize: the six enemies first, desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, then whatever else yours are.
Pick the one that showed up most this week, look it in the face without fighting it, and say its name quietly, inside. When it grows back, and it will, you'll recognize it faster.

wordCard.voice: Ravana, the one who made the worlds cry out: the great, learned, ten-headed king, out of people to send, finally facing Rama himself.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Ravana. The Uttara Kanda explains the name as 'the one who made the worlds cry out'.

carryVoice: Your line: six inner enemies, and they grow back. Naming one is the first arrow. That's day sixty-five in the books.
